lessons.title: Your first pan
lessons.subtitle: Heat, oil and how to tell it's ready
lessons.coverBrief: Top-down overhead photo, camera pointing straight down, of one black cast-iron frying pan holding three thick slices of halloumi seared deep golden brown in a thin film of shimmering oil, beside one plain matte white round ceramic plate holding two more seared golden halloumi slices, on a seamless pale cream background, soft diffused daylight, faint soft shadow. Nothing else in frame. 3:2 landscape, photorealistic editorial food photography, sharp, natural colours.

left.caption: Non-stick: eggs, pancakes and fish, on medium heat or lower
left.alt: An empty black non-stick frying pan with a silicone spatula resting in it

right.caption: Cast iron or steel: searing and browning; slow to heat, holds it
right.alt: An empty black cast-iron frying pan with a smooth, lightly oiled surface

pages.headline: What the dial means
pages.body: On a 1–9 dial, low (2–3) melts butter and softens onions over 8–10 minutes. Medium (4–6) cooks most things. High (7–9) sears and stir-fries in 2–5 minutes, so stay by the pan.

steps.text: Heat a dry steel or cast-iron pan on medium for 2 minutes.
Flick in 3–4 drops of water from your fingertips.
They sit and steam? Give it 1 more minute.
They hiss and vanish in 1–2 seconds? Medium-hot, right for most cooking.
They bead up and skate like marbles? Hot enough to sear: add 1 tablespoon of oil.

pages.headline: Oil is ready when it shimmers
pages.body: Add 1 tablespoon of oil to the hot pan and give it 30–60 seconds. Ready: it runs thin like water and ripples in the light. A first wisp of smoke means very hot; steady smoke means too hot: lift the pan off for 1 minute.
pages.alt: Shimmering oil with a first wisp of smoke in a black cast-iron pan

pages.headline: Why food sticks, and the fix

steps.text: Pan too cold: heat it 2 minutes before the oil goes in.
Food too wet: pat chicken, tofu or halloumi dry with 2 sheets of kitchen paper.
Too little oil: use 1 tablespoon for a 24 cm (9 in) pan.
Moved too soon: leave it 2–3 minutes; it lets go once the underside browns.

pages.headline: Leave it alone and it lets go
pages.body: Lay the pieces in with 2 cm between them and don't touch them for 2–3 minutes. Food sticks at first, then releases as a golden crust forms. Lift 1 corner with a spatula: if it clings, give it 1 minute more.
pages.alt: Six thick halloumi slices with deep golden-brown tops in a black cast-iron pan

pages.question: You flick water into a steel pan and the drops just sit and steam. What next?
pages.explanation: Sitting drops mean the pan is still too cool, so wait until they bead up and skate.

pages.text: Hot pan, then oil, then food, and leave it 2–3 minutes before you move it.

lessons.title: Knife basics
lessons.subtitle: Grip, claw, and three cuts you'll use daily
lessons.coverBrief: Top-down overhead photo, camera pointing straight down, of one plain matte white round ceramic plate holding three neat heaps side by side: thin half-moon slices of raw red onion, even 1 cm cubes of raw carrot and a small pile of finely minced raw garlic, on a seamless pale cream background, soft diffused daylight, faint soft shadow. Nothing else in frame. 3:2 landscape, photorealistic editorial food photography, sharp, natural colours.

pages.headline: Set up, then hold the knife

steps.text: Lay 1 damp sheet of kitchen paper under the board so it can't slide.
Wrap 3 fingers round the handle.
Pinch the blade just past the handle with your thumb and 1 bent finger.
Keep the tip on the board and rock the blade down and forward, 1 stroke a cut.

pages.headline: The claw keeps fingertips clear
pages.body: Curl the fingertips of the hand holding the food under, with your thumb tucked behind them. Rest the flat of the blade against your knuckles and slide your hand back 2–3 mm after each cut. For round things, halve them first so they sit flat.
pages.alt: A hand in the claw grip holding a carrot against a chef's knife

pages.headline: Slice: flat side down, 2–3 mm
pages.body: Cut a thin piece off one side so the food sits flat and still. Then slice straight down, 2–3 mm (⅛ in) thick, moving your claw back after each cut. Halve an onion root to tip for half-moons, or slice it whole for rings.
pages.alt: Thin, even red onion slices in half-moons and rings on a wooden board

left.caption: Dice: even cubes, so every piece cooks at the same rate
left.alt: A neat pile of even diced sweet potato cubes on a wooden board

right.caption: Mince: rock the blade over garlic or herbs, almost to a paste
right.alt: Finely minced garlic beside two peeled cloves on a wooden board

steps.text: Halve 1 onion from root to tip, peel it, and keep the root on.
Lay a half flat; cut lengthways every 5 mm, stopping 1 cm short of the root.
Cut across those lines every 5 mm, and the dice falls away.
Stop 1 cm from the root and throw the root end away.

pages.headline: A separate board for raw meat
pages.body: FSIS suggests one board for fresh produce and bread and a separate one for raw meat, poultry and seafood, so raw juices never reach food that won't be cooked. Wash both in hot, soapy water after each use.
pages.alt: Two raw chicken breasts on a separate red chopping board beside a knife

pages.question: In the claw grip, what does the flat of the blade rest against?
pages.explanation: Knuckles guide the blade while your fingertips stay curled back, out of the edge's way.

pages.text: Steady board, pinch grip and a claw hand, then slice, dice or mince to an even size.

lessons.title: Salt, fat, acid
lessons.subtitle: Why food tastes flat, and the three fixes
lessons.coverBrief: Top-down overhead photo, camera pointing straight down, of three small plain matte white round ceramic bowls in a neat row: one of flaky white sea salt, one of golden extra virgin olive oil, and one holding two halves of a fresh lemon, cut side up, on a seamless pale cream background, soft diffused daylight, faint soft shadows. Nothing else in frame. 3:2 landscape, photorealistic editorial food photography, sharp, natural colours.

pages.headline: Flat food is missing one of three
pages.body: When a dish tastes dull, the fix is usually salt, fat or acid. Salt makes every flavour louder. Fat carries flavour and makes food feel rich. Acid, from lemon or vinegar, makes it bright. Taste 1 spoonful and ask which one it needs.
pages.alt: Tomato sauce in a pan, a tasting spoon on the rim, sea salt beside it

pages.headline: Salt in stages, starting early
pages.body: Salt at the start seasons food all the way through; salt only at the end sits on the surface. Start with ¼ teaspoon on the onions for a dish for 2, ¼ teaspoon more when the liquid goes in, then taste before adding any more.
pages.alt: Soft, pale chopped onion glistening with oil in a steel frying pan

pages.headline: Most salt is already in the food
pages.body: The NHS's maximum for anyone 11 or over is 6 g of salt a day, about 1 level teaspoon, counting what's already in food. Around three quarters comes from bought foods like bread, breakfast cereal and ready meals, so taste before you add more.

pages.headline: Fat carries flavour
pages.body: Spices release their flavour into hot fat. Warm 1 teaspoon of cumin seeds in 1 tablespoon of oil for 30–60 seconds, until they sizzle and smell toasty, before the onions go in. A dry salad or plain veg? 1 teaspoon of olive oil per serving.
pages.alt: Cumin seeds and a bay leaf sizzling in shimmering oil in a steel pot

pages.headline: Acid wakes up heavy food
pages.body: If a dish is salted but still tastes heavy, it needs acid. Stir in 1 teaspoon of lemon juice or vinegar per 2 servings at the end, taste, and add 1 more if it's still heavy. Lentils, tomato sauce, soups and roast veg all brighten.
pages.alt: A halved lemon beside a small white bowl of lemon juice on a board

steps.text: Taste 1 spoonful on a clean spoon, not the one you stir with.
Flat or dull? Add 1 pinch of salt, stir 30 seconds, taste again.
Heavy? Add ½ teaspoon (2–3 ml) of lemon juice or vinegar.
Thin or sharp? Stir in 1 teaspoon of olive oil or butter.
Too salty? Stir in 100 ml of water or unsalted stock and simmer 2 minutes.

pages.question: Your soup has its salt but still tastes heavy and dull. What helps first?
pages.explanation: Acid brightens a dish that already has its salt; more salt makes it salty and water makes it thinner.

pages.text: Taste before you serve: flat needs salt, heavy needs acid, thin or sharp needs fat.

lessons.title: Eggs five ways
lessons.subtitle: Boiled, scrambled, fried, omelette and poached
lessons.coverBrief: Top-down overhead photo, camera pointing straight down, of one plain matte white round ceramic plate holding eggs cooked four ways: a halved jammy boiled egg, a fried egg with a fully set white and a soft golden yolk, a neat poached egg with a firm white, and a small heap of soft golden scrambled egg, on a seamless pale cream background, soft diffused daylight, faint soft shadow. Nothing else in frame. 3:2 landscape, photorealistic editorial food photography, sharp, natural colours.

pages.headline: Boiled: 6, 8 or 10 minutes
pages.body: Lower large eggs straight from the fridge into gently boiling water with a spoon. 6 minutes gives a runny yolk, 8 a jammy one, 10 a firm one. Then 2 minutes in cold water so they stop cooking and you can peel them easily.
pages.alt: Three halved boiled eggs with runny, jammy and firm yolks on a white plate

pages.headline: Scrambled: low and slow
pages.body: Beat 2 eggs with 1 pinch of salt. Melt 10 g butter on low heat, pour the eggs in and push them to the middle every 10 seconds. Off the heat at 4–5 minutes, once no liquid egg is left but the curds still shine.
pages.alt: Soft, glossy golden scrambled egg curds in a black non-stick pan

pages.headline: Fried: medium heat, set white
pages.body: Heat 1 teaspoon of oil in a non-stick pan on medium for 1 minute. Crack the egg in and cook 2–3 minutes, until the white is opaque right up to the yolk. For a firmer top, put a lid on for the last 1 minute.
pages.alt: A fried egg with a set white and soft golden yolk in a non-stick pan

pages.headline: Omelette: pull, tilt, fold
pages.body: Beat 3 eggs. Melt 10 g butter on medium until it foams and pour them in. For 1 minute, pull the edges to the middle and tilt so raw egg fills the gaps. At 2–3 minutes, with the top set, fill one half and fold.
pages.alt: A golden folded omelette with red pepper, spinach and feta in a cast-iron pan

pages.headline: Poached: a bare simmer, 3–4 minutes
pages.body: Heat 8 cm of water to a bare simmer: tiny bubbles only. Crack 1 egg into a cup, swirl the water slowly and tip the egg into the middle. After 3–4 minutes, once the white is set, lift it out with a slotted spoon.
pages.alt: Four white poached eggs drifting in barely simmering water in a steel pot

source.name: NHS Foods to avoid in pregnancy

pages.headline: A runny yolk? Check the stamp
pages.body: The NHS says UK hen eggs with the red British Lion stamp, or the Laid in Britain logo, can be eaten runny before their use-by date, even in pregnancy. In pregnancy, it advises eating other hen eggs, and duck, goose or quail eggs, only well-cooked.
pages.alt: Avocado toast topped with two poached eggs, one yolk running, on a white plate

pages.question: A large egg goes from the fridge into boiling water. How long for a jammy yolk?
pages.explanation: 6 minutes gives runny, 8 jammy and 10 firm, then 2 minutes in cold water.

pages.text: Boiled 6 · 8 · 10, scrambled low and slow, poached at a bare simmer.

lessons.title: Rice and pasta, right every time
lessons.subtitle: Absorption, salted water, al dente and the rice rule
lessons.coverBrief: Top-down overhead photo, camera pointing straight down, of two plain matte white round ceramic bowls side by side, one holding fluffy cooked white basmati rice with separate grains, the other a neatly twirled nest of glossy cooked spaghetti, on a seamless pale cream background, soft diffused daylight, faint soft shadows. Nothing else in frame. 3:2 landscape, photorealistic editorial food photography, sharp, natural colours.

steps.text: Rinse 150 g of rice in cold water 3 times, until it runs nearly clear.
Bring it to the boil with 240 ml of water and 1 pinch of salt.
Lid on, lowest heat, 12 minutes, and don't lift the lid.
Off the heat, lid still on, rest 5–10 minutes, then fluff with a fork.

pages.headline: How to tell it's done
pages.body: After 12 minutes, small holes dot the surface and no water shows when you tilt the pan. Still wet? Lid back on for 2 minutes. Too firm with the water gone? Add 2 tablespoons of boiling water and give it 3 minutes more.
pages.alt: Cooked white rice in a steel pot, its surface dotted with steam holes

pages.headline: Pasta: plenty of water, salted
pages.body: Use 1 litre of water for every 100 g of pasta, so it moves freely and doesn't clump. When it's at a rolling boil, add 1 teaspoon of salt per litre, then the pasta, and stir for the first 1 minute.
pages.alt: A steel pot of water at a rolling boil beside a dish of sea salt

pages.headline: Al dente: tender, with bite
pages.body: Start tasting 1 minute before the packet time. Bite a piece and look at the cut edge: ready when it's no longer chalky but still firm, with a tiny pale dot in the middle. Scoop out 1 mug (250 ml) of the water, then drain.
pages.alt: A halved rigatoni showing a tiny firm pale core, beside drained pasta

pages.headline: The rice rule
pages.body: Spores in rice can survive cooking. Left at room temperature, they grow into bacteria that can make you sick, and reheating won't undo it. The NHS advises cooling it within 1 hour, keeping it in the fridge and eating it within 24 hours.
pages.alt: Fluffy white rice steaming in a steel saucepan

pages.headline: Keeping cooked rice, step by step

steps.text: Spread leftover rice in 1 shallow box so it cools within 1 hour.
Into the fridge, and eat it within 24 hours.
Reheat it once only, until steaming hot: 70 °C (158 °F) for 2 minutes in the middle.
Left out for 1 night at room temperature? Throw it away, even if it looks fine.

pages.question: You cooked rice at 7 pm for tomorrow's lunch. When does it go in the fridge?
pages.explanation: The NHS advises cooling cooked rice within 1 hour, then keeping it in the fridge and eating it within 24 hours.

pages.text: Rice: absorb, rest, then chill within 1 hour; pasta: salted water, tasted 1 minute early.

lessons.title: Chicken, safely and juicy
lessons.subtitle: One number, a short rest, and no washing
lessons.coverBrief: Top-down overhead photo, camera pointing straight down, of one plain matte white round ceramic plate holding a golden pan-seared chicken breast cut in half to show moist white meat all the way through, beside a golden roasted chicken thigh, fully cooked, on a seamless pale cream background, soft diffused daylight, faint soft shadow. Nothing else in frame. 3:2 landscape, photorealistic editorial food photography, sharp, natural colours.

source.name: FSIS Safe minimum internal temperature chart

pages.headline: 74 °C (165 °F) is the number
pages.body: FSIS's minimum for all chicken, from breasts and thighs to wings and mince, is 74 °C (165 °F), measured with a food thermometer before it comes off the heat. Cook it hotter if you like, never cooler.
pages.alt: A probe thermometer in the thickest part of a golden roast chicken leg

pages.headline: Check the thickest part
pages.body: Push the probe into the thickest part, away from bone; on a thin breast, go in from the side to the middle. FSIS says colour isn't a reliable sign of doneness: only a thermometer shows it's reached 74 °C (165 °F).
pages.alt: A probe thermometer pushed into the side of a golden chicken breast

source.name: FSIS Chicken from farm to table

pages.headline: Breast or thigh: how long to roast

left.caption: Boneless breast, 115 g, at 180 °C (160 °C fan, 350 °F)
left.alt: Three golden roasted chicken breasts among cherry tomatoes and white beans

right.caption: Thigh, 115–225 g, at 180 °C (160 °C fan, 350 °F)
right.alt: Eight golden roasted chicken thighs over crisp potato wedges and peppers

source.name: FSIS Safe minimum internal temperature chart

pages.headline: A juicy breast in the pan

steps.text: Flatten 1 breast to an even 2 cm with a rolling pin, between 2 sheets of baking paper.
Pat it dry with 2 sheets of kitchen paper; salt both sides with ¼ teaspoon.
Medium-high heat, 1 tablespoon of oil, 5–6 minutes a side, to 74 °C (165 °F) inside.
Boneless thighs: 6–7 minutes a side; 2 extra minutes won't dry them out.

pages.headline: Rest it 5 minutes
pages.body: Move cooked chicken to a board and leave it 5 minutes before you slice it, or 15 minutes for a whole bird, loosely covered with foil. The juices settle back into the meat instead of running out across the board.
pages.alt: Grilled chicken fillets sliced on a board, juicy and white inside

source.name: FSIS Chicken from farm to table

pages.headline: Don't wash raw chicken
pages.body: Rinsing doesn't remove bacteria; only cooking kills them. FSIS says washing raw chicken spreads its juices to the sink, worktop and nearby food. Take it straight from the pack to the tray or pan, then wash your hands with soap for 20 seconds.
pages.alt: Raw chicken thighs laid over half-roasted potato wedges in a baking tray

source.name: FSIS Chicken from farm to table

pages.question: Cooked chicken looks slightly pink near the bone. What tells you it's cooked?
pages.explanation: FSIS says colour isn't a sign of doneness: only a thermometer shows the 74 °C (165 °F) minimum.

source.name: FSIS Chicken from farm to table

pages.text: Cook chicken to 74 °C (165 °F) in the thickest part, rest it 5 minutes, and never wash it raw.

lessons.title: Vegetables that taste good
lessons.subtitle: A hot oven, room on the tray, salt and lemon
lessons.coverBrief: Top-down overhead photo, camera pointing straight down, of one plain matte white round ceramic plate heaped with roasted vegetables with browned, crisp edges: broccoli florets, red pepper chunks, red onion wedges and courgette half-moons, glossy with olive oil, a halved lemon at the rim, on a seamless pale cream background, soft diffused daylight, faint soft shadow. Nothing else in frame. 3:2 landscape, photorealistic editorial food photography, sharp, natural colours.

pages.headline: A hot oven browns the edges
pages.body: Heat the oven to 220 °C (200 °C fan, 425 °F) for 15 minutes before the tray goes in. At that heat, the edges brown and turn sweet while the middle turns tender, in 20–30 minutes for most veg cut to 3 cm.
pages.alt: Charred red pepper, caramelised carrot and red onion on a dark baking tray

left.caption: Piled 3 deep: the water can't escape, so they steam
left.alt: Pale, steamed broccoli, courgette and pepper piled deep in a white dish

right.caption: 1 layer with gaps, or 2 trays: the edges brown
right.alt: Two trays of browned aubergine, courgette, pepper, red onion and chickpeas

pages.headline: Oil and salt go on first
pages.body: Cut the veg into even 3 cm pieces. For 500 g, toss with 1 tablespoon of oil and ½ teaspoon of salt in a bowl, so every piece is coated, then spread them out cut side down. Turn them once, halfway through.
pages.alt: Raw veg chunks and chickpeas, glossy with oil and spice, on two trays

pages.headline: Roasting times, cut to 3 cm
pages.body: At 220 °C (200 °C fan, 425 °F), in 1 layer, turned once halfway. Start checking 5 minutes early: they're ready when a knife slides in and the edges are brown.

pages.headline: 80 g counts as 1 portion
pages.body: The NHS counts 80 g of fresh, frozen or tinned veg as 1 portion of your 5 A Day, on its own or in a dish. Sweet potatoes and parsnips count; potatoes don't, as they're the starchy part of a meal.
pages.alt: Golden roasted sweet potato, red onion and red pepper on a lined tray

pages.headline: Finish with acid and herbs
pages.body: Straight out of the oven, squeeze ½ lemon or sprinkle 1 teaspoon of vinegar over a tray for 2, then add 1 tablespoon of chopped parsley or mint. The sharpness cuts through the sweet, browned edges and makes the flavour pop.
pages.alt: Rocket, mint, blistered red pepper and chickpeas glossy with lemon dressing

pages.question: Your roast veg came out pale and soft. What's the most likely cause?
pages.explanation: Piled-up veg steam in their own water; 1 layer with gaps, or 2 trays, lets the edges brown.

pages.text: Hot oven, 1 layer with room, salt before and lemon after.

lessons.title: Batch cooking
lessons.subtitle: Cool fast, label it, reheat until steaming, freeze the rest
lessons.coverBrief: Top-down overhead photo, camera pointing straight down, of four plain matte white round ceramic bowls in a neat square, each holding an equal portion of thick reddish-brown chicken thigh curry beside a mound of fluffy white basmati rice, scattered with coriander leaves, on a seamless pale cream background, soft diffused daylight, faint soft shadows. Nothing else in frame. 3:2 landscape, photorealistic editorial food photography, sharp, natural colours.

pages.headline: Cook dishes that keep, and label them
pages.body: Curries, chillies, stews, soups and roast veg reheat well: cook 4 portions in a single 1-hour session. Make crisp things, dressed salads and rice on the day you eat them. Write the dish and date on every lid with 1 strip of tape.
pages.alt: Chicken thigh curry beside fluffy basmati rice in a white bowl

pages.headline: Into the fridge within 2 hours
pages.body: FSIS says to get cooked food into the fridge within 2 hours. A big pot takes a long time to cool, so split it into shallow boxes, 1 portion each. Hot food can go straight into the fridge.
pages.alt: Four shallow boxes of chicken curry spread flat to cool, lids beside them

steps.text: In the fridge: eat it within 3–4 days.
In the freezer: most leftovers are best within 3–4 months, then slowly dry out.
Thawed in the fridge? Eat it within 3–4 days.

pages.headline: Reheat to at least 74 °C (165 °F)
pages.body: FSIS says leftovers need to reach at least 74 °C (165 °F) in the middle, and soups, sauces and gravies a rolling boil. Cover the dish, and stir or turn it halfway in the microwave: microwaves leave cold spots, so check 2–3 places.
pages.alt: A white bowl of reheated vegetable curry with steam rising from the middle

pages.headline: What freezes, and what doesn't
pages.body: Almost anything freezes, FSIS says, but mayonnaise, cream sauces and lettuce come back poor, and eggs in their shells don't go in at all. Soups and stews keep their best for 2–3 months. Freeze flat bags in 1 layer, then stack them once solid.
pages.alt: Three flat sealed freezer bags of frozen tomato soup side by side

pages.headline: Thaw cold, never on the counter

steps.text: Fridge: 1 night for a single portion, 1–2 days for most bigger boxes.
Faster: sealed bag in cold water, changed every 30 minutes, then cook it at once.
Or reheat straight from frozen, allowing about 1½ times as long.

pages.question: Which of these freezes worst?
pages.explanation: FSIS lists cream sauce, mayonnaise and lettuce as foods that don't freeze well, while soups and stews keep for 2–3 months.

pages.text: Fridge within 2 hours, a date on every lid, and reheat to at least 74 °C (165 °F).

lessons.title: What a calorie is
lessons.subtitle: Energy in food, and what 2,000 kcal looks like
lessons.coverBrief: Top-down overhead photo, camera pointing straight down, of one plain matte white round ceramic plate holding five everyday foods in neat separate heaps: a sliced ripe banana, a small heap of whole almonds, a halved hard-boiled egg with a set yellow yolk, one slice of wholemeal toast and a small mound of cooked white rice. The plate is centred on a seamless pale cream background, soft diffused daylight, faint soft shadow under the plate. Nothing else in frame. 3:2 landscape, photorealistic editorial food photography, sharp, natural colours.

pages.headline: A calorie is a unit of energy
pages.body: Food and drink give your body the energy it runs on. That energy is counted in calories: labels write kcal, short for kilocalories, and kJ, short for kilojoules.
pages.alt: Bulgur topped with roast chicken thigh, charred courgette and red pepper

pages.headline: Energy in 1 g of each
pages.body: Fat gives 9 kcal (37 kJ) a gram, whether saturated or unsaturated. Carbohydrate and protein give 4 kcal (17 kJ). That's why oil and butter hold so much energy for their size.

source.name: NHS My Health London: calories in food and drink

pages.headline: Two smoothies, almost double the energy

left.caption: Spinach, mango, milk and fat-free Greek yoghurt
left.alt: A pale green spinach and mango smoothie

right.caption: Banana, oats, soya yoghurt and peanut butter
right.alt: A creamy beige peanut butter and banana smoothie

left.caption: Lentil soup: 23 g fibre, 26 g protein
left.alt: Smooth orange lentil soup topped with pumpkin seeds

right.caption: Turkey meatballs: 8 g fibre, 37 g protein
right.alt: Turkey meatballs in tomato sauce beside green beans

pages.headline: What 2,000 kcal can look like
pages.body: Four Clara servings, from breakfast to an evening snack, come to 2,007 kcal. Energy needs differ with your age, height, weight and how active you are.

source.name: NHS My Health London: food labels

pages.headline: How labels use 2,000 kcal
pages.body: Front-of-pack labels show energy as a share of an adult's reference intake: 8,400 kJ or 2,000 kcal. A serving of Clara's butter chicken with rice is 704 kcal, or 35%. It's a yardstick, not a target.

pages.question: Gram for gram, which gives the most energy?
pages.explanation: Fat gives 9 kcal a gram, more than twice the 4 kcal in protein or carbohydrate.

pages.text: A calorie measures energy: the number says how much, not what else the food brings.

lessons.title: Protein
lessons.subtitle: Why your body needs it, how much, and where
lessons.coverBrief: Top-down overhead photo, camera pointing straight down, of four small plain matte white round ceramic plates and bowls in a neat row: one small cooked chicken breast cut into thick slices, fully cooked and opaque; three hard-boiled eggs halved to show set yellow yolks; a bowl of thick white Greek yoghurt; a bowl of baked beans in orange tomato sauce. On a seamless pale cream background, soft diffused daylight, faint soft shadows. Nothing else in frame. 3:2 landscape, photorealistic editorial food photography, sharp, natural colours.

pages.headline: Your body is built with protein
pages.body: Protein is in your muscle, bone, skin and hair, and in the enzymes that run your body's chemistry. It's made of 20-plus building blocks called amino acids, and 9 of them come only from food.
pages.alt: A folded omelette with feta, spinach and red pepper

source.name: BDA Food Fact Sheet: Sport and exercise

pages.headline: Protein a day for a 60 kg adult
pages.body: For adults who don't exercise, it's about 0.75 g a day for each kg of body weight. Strength and endurance athletes need about 1.4–2.0 g a kg.

source.name: BDA Food Fact Sheet: Sport and exercise

pages.headline: About 20 g of protein in each
pages.body: Weights are as eaten. Three medium eggs, a pint (600 ml) of semi-skimmed milk or 100 g of unsalted nuts or seeds also give about 20 g.

source.name: BDA Food Fact Sheet: Sport and exercise

pages.headline: Two breakfasts, 13 g of protein apart

left.caption: Skyr with raspberries, toasted oats and almonds
left.alt: Thick white skyr swirled with raspberries and toasted oats

right.caption: Overnight oats with chia, hemp seeds and berries
right.alt: Creamy overnight oats topped with blueberries and seeds

pages.headline: Plants bring protein too
pages.body: A cup of cooked lentils gives about 18 g of protein and 15 g of fibre. Plant foods differ in their amino acids, so a mix of beans, lentils, grains, nuts and seeds over the day covers them all.
pages.alt: Golden dal with wilted spinach beside basmati rice

source.name: BDA Food Fact Sheet: Sport and exercise

pages.question: Which of these gives about 20 g of protein?
options: A pint (600 ml) of semi-skimmed milk
pages.explanation: A pint of semi-skimmed milk gives about 20 g, as much as 3 medium eggs.

pages.question: How many amino acids come only from food?
pages.explanation: Your body makes the rest; these 9 are called the essential amino acids.

source.name: BDA Food Fact Sheet: Sport and exercise

pages.text: Protein builds your body: 3 eggs, a small chicken breast or a pint of milk each give about 20 g.

lessons.title: Carbs aren't the enemy
lessons.subtitle: Fibre, whole grains and glycaemic load in plain words
lessons.coverBrief: Top-down overhead photo, camera pointing straight down, of one plain matte white round ceramic plate divided into four neat sections: a twirled nest of cooked wholewheat spaghetti, a baked potato split open with its crisp brown skin on, a slice of seeded wholemeal bread, and a mound of cooked brown rice. The plate is centred on a seamless pale cream background, soft diffused daylight, faint soft shadow under the plate. Nothing else in frame. 3:2 landscape, photorealistic editorial food photography, sharp, natural colours.

pages.headline: Starchy foods: energy and much more
pages.body: Potatoes, bread, rice, pasta and cereals are your main source of carbohydrate. Besides energy, they bring fibre, calcium, iron and B vitamins. The NHS puts starchy foods at just over a third of what you eat.
pages.alt: Wholewheat spaghetti in a thick lentil ragù

pages.question: Gram for gram, how much energy does starchy food have, compared with fat?
pages.explanation: Starch has fewer than half the kcal of fat, gram for gram; butter or oil added in cooking raises it.

pages.headline: Whole grains keep all three parts
pages.body: A whole grain has its fibre-rich bran, its nutrient-packed germ and its starchy endosperm. Milling often strips the bran and germ for a whiter flour or rice, so whole grains can hold up to 75% more nutrients.
pages.alt: A slice of wholemeal bread beside a slice of white bread

pages.question: Which word on a pack tells you the grain is whole?
pages.explanation: Multigrain only means more than one grain; look for 'whole' before the grain's name.

source.name: Harvard Nutrition Source: Carbohydrates and blood sugar

pages.headline: How fast a carb raises blood sugar
pages.body: The glycaemic index (GI) rates carb foods from 0 to 100. White bread digests fast and scores high; whole oats digest slowly, so blood sugar rises more gently.

source.name: Harvard Nutrition Source: Carbohydrates and blood sugar

pages.headline: Glycaemic load counts the portion too
pages.body: GI doesn't say how much carb a portion holds; glycaemic load multiplies the two. Lentils, beans and apples are low. Brown rice, porridge and wholegrain bread are medium. A baked potato or a cup of white basmati rice is high.

pages.headline: Keep the skins on your potatoes
pages.body: In the UK, potatoes count as the starchy part of a meal, not one of your 5 A Day. They bring fibre, B vitamins and potassium, and leaving the skin on keeps more of the fibre and vitamins.
pages.alt: Seared cod with crushed new potatoes and green beans

pages.text: Carbs are fuel: whole grains, pulses and potatoes in their skins bring fibre and a gentler rise.

lessons.title: Fat
lessons.subtitle: The kinds, the amounts, and which oil for what
lessons.coverBrief: Top-down overhead photo, camera pointing straight down, of one plain matte white round ceramic plate holding a halved ripe avocado with its stone in one half, a small heap of whole walnuts and almonds, a pan-seared salmon fillet with golden crisp skin, fully cooked and opaque, and a small plain white ceramic dish of golden olive oil. The plate is centred on a seamless pale cream background, soft diffused daylight, faint soft shadow under the plate. Nothing else in frame. 3:2 landscape, photorealistic editorial food photography, sharp, natural colours.

pages.headline: Your body needs some fat
pages.body: Fat gives essential fatty acids your body can't make, and it helps you absorb vitamins A, D and E. Every kind is energy-dense: 9 kcal a gram, saturated or unsaturated, against 4 for carbs and protein.
pages.alt: Avocado on toasted sourdough topped with two poached eggs

source.name: Harvard Nutrition Source: Types of fat

pages.headline: How much of each fat is saturated
pages.body: Every fat is a mix. Plant oils are mostly unsaturated; butter and coconut oil are mostly saturated. Each bar is the saturated share of that fat's total.

pages.headline: Unsaturated fats: plants and oily fish
pages.body: Monounsaturated fats are in olive and rapeseed oil, avocados, almonds and peanuts. Omega-3, a polyunsaturated kind, comes from oily fish such as salmon and mackerel. Swapping some saturated fat for these can help lower LDL cholesterol.
pages.alt: Pan-seared salmon with new potatoes and cucumber salad

pages.headline: UK fat guidance for adults, a day
pages.body: UK guidance puts fat at about a third of daily energy, mostly unsaturated, and saturated fat at no more than a tenth. These are adult figures.

pages.headline: Reading fat on a label
pages.body: For saturated fat, low is 1.5 g or less per 100 g and high is more than 5 g. On front-of-pack colours, high shows red and low shows green.

source.name: Harvard Nutrition Source: Ask the expert, canola oil

pages.headline: Which oil for what
pages.body: Olive and rapeseed oil cover cooking, salads and the table. Extra virgin olive oil earns its place where you taste it. A tablespoon is about 14 g of oil. Burnt oil loses its taste and its useful fats.
pages.alt: Two small white bowls of oil, pale rapeseed and green-gold olive

source.name: Harvard Nutrition Source: Types of fat

pages.question: Which of these fats is mostly unsaturated?
pages.explanation: Only 7% of rapeseed oil's fat is saturated, against 60% for butter and 87% for coconut oil.

pages.text: All fat is energy-dense; plant oils, nuts, seeds and oily fish bring the unsaturated kinds.

lessons.title: Fibre
lessons.subtitle: The 30 g target and five ways to get there
lessons.coverBrief: Top-down overhead photo, camera pointing straight down, of one plain matte white round ceramic plate holding neat separate heaps of fibre-rich foods: rolled oats, cooked green lentils, drained chickpeas, fresh raspberries, a halved ripe pear and small steamed broccoli florets, bright green. The plate is centred on a seamless pale cream background, soft diffused daylight, faint soft shadow under the plate. Nothing else in frame. 3:2 landscape, photorealistic editorial food photography, sharp, natural colours.

pages.headline: Fibre is the plant part you don't digest
pages.body: Fibre passes through your small intestine undigested; bacteria in your large intestine break it down. Your gut needs it to work normally, and a high-fibre diet is linked with lower risk of heart disease, type 2 diabetes and bowel cancer.
pages.alt: Puy lentils and bulgur with roasted peppers, courgette and chickpeas

source.name: NHS: How to get more fibre into your diet

pages.headline: Fibre a day, by age
pages.body: Most adults get about 20 g a day, and 11 to 18-year-olds about 16 g.

steps.text: Start the day with 50 g of porridge oats: about 4 g of fibre.
Swap to 2 slices of wholemeal bread: about 7 g.
Eat a 180 g baked potato with its skin: about 5 g.
Add 80 g of baked beans: about 3 g.
Top with 40–50 g of walnuts or almonds: about 4 g.

source.name: NHS: How to get more fibre into your diet

pages.headline: Three meals, about 30 g of fibre
pages.body: The NHS example day: 2 slices of wholemeal toast with peanut butter and an orange, wholemeal spaghetti with lentil and tomato sauce, then chicken with a skin-on baked potato, carrots and green beans.

pages.headline: Two curries, 18 g of fibre apart

left.caption: Butter chicken with basmati rice
left.alt: Creamy orange butter chicken beside basmati rice

right.caption: Chickpea curry with basmati rice
right.alt: Russet chickpea curry half-covering basmati rice

pages.headline: Fibre works best with time and water
pages.body: Adding fibre gradually gives your gut time to adjust, with less bloating and gas. Fibre also draws water into the bowel, so fluid matters more as fibre goes up.
pages.alt: Tomato vegetable soup with cannellini and borlotti beans and pasta

pages.question: On a UK label, how much fibre per 100 g makes a food 'high fibre'?
pages.explanation: High fibre is 6 g or more per 100 g; 'source of fibre' is 3 g or more.

source.name: NHS: How to get more fibre into your diet

pages.text: Adults need about 30 g of fibre a day: whole grains, potato skins, pulses, nuts and fruit add up.

lessons.title: Sugar
lessons.subtitle: Added or natural, and how to spot it
lessons.coverBrief: Top-down overhead photo, camera pointing straight down, of one plain matte white round ceramic plate holding one whole unpeeled orange, one peeled orange pulled apart into segments, and a small neat stack of six white sugar cubes, on a seamless pale cream background, soft diffused daylight, faint soft shadow under the plate. Nothing else in frame. 3:2 landscape, photorealistic editorial food photography, sharp, natural colours.

pages.headline: Not all sugar counts the same
pages.body: Free sugars are added to food and drinks, or come from honey, syrups and juice. Sugars inside milk, whole fruit and vegetables aren't free sugars. In this bowl, you get sugars from apple, berries and cottage cheese, but no free sugars.
pages.alt: Cottage cheese topped with warm apple, blueberries and seeds

left.caption: Mango and spinach, whole, before blending
left.alt: Spinach leaves, frozen mango, yoghurt, ginger and lime on a board

right.caption: The same mango, blended into a smoothie
right.alt: A pale green spinach and mango smoothie in a glass

pages.question: Which of these is a free sugar?
options: The sugar in a whole apple
The sugar in a glass of milk
pages.explanation: Juicing releases fruit's sugars, so they count as free sugars; the sugars in whole fruit and milk don't.

pages.headline: One can of cola, in sugar cubes
pages.body: The NHS puts adults' free sugars at 30 g a day at most, about 7 cubes. One can of cola can hold up to 9. For juice and smoothies together, its limit is 150 ml a day.

pages.headline: The per 100 g trick
pages.body: A label's “of which sugars” is all sugars, free or not, so it can't show added sugar alone. It's still a useful way to compare: 5 g or less per 100 g is low, more than 22.5 g is high.

pages.headline: Spotting added sugar on the pack

steps.text: Read the first 3 ingredients: sugar near the top means the food is likely high in free sugars.
Know its other names: the NHS lists more than 15, from glucose to treacle.
Count honey, syrups and fruit juice concentrate too: all 3 are free sugars.

pages.question: A yoghurt has 12 g of sugars per 100 g. Where does that sit?
pages.explanation: Between 5 g and 22.5 g of sugars per 100 g counts as medium.

pages.text: Free sugars are added sugar, honey, syrups and juice — not the sugar inside whole fruit or milk.

lessons.title: Ultra-processed
lessons.subtitle: What NOVA means, and why it's easy to eat more
lessons.coverBrief: Top-down overhead photo, camera pointing straight down, of three small plain matte white round ceramic bowls in a neat row: the first holds two whole raw unpeeled potatoes, the second holds chunks of boiled potato with the skin on, the third holds plain ridged potato crisps, on a seamless pale cream background, soft diffused daylight, faint soft shadows under the bowls. Nothing else in frame. 3:2 landscape, photorealistic editorial food photography, sharp, natural colours.

source.name: Harvard Nutrition Source: Processed foods and health

pages.headline: NOVA sorts food into 4 groups
pages.body: Group 4, ultra-processed, takes several processing steps and many ingredients, often with additives such as flavourings, emulsifiers, preservatives and sweeteners.

pages.headline: Ingredients you wouldn't have at home
pages.body: Ultra-processed foods often hold ingredients you'd not usually keep at home, such as preservatives, sweeteners and emulsifiers. The NHS's examples include sweetened drinks, crisps, packaged cakes and biscuits, ice cream, sweets and some ready meals.
pages.alt: Sponge cake, two biscuits and gummy sweets on a white plate

source.name: Harvard Nutrition Source: Processed foods and health

pages.headline: Why it's easy to eat more
pages.body: In a 2019 trial, 20 adults spent 14 days on an ultra-processed diet and 14 on an unprocessed one, eating as much as they liked. On the first they ate about 500 kcal more a day, and faster, yet felt no hungrier or fuller.

pages.headline: Processed isn't one thing
pages.body: Not all processed foods are unhealthy. Some ultra-processed ones can be part of a healthy diet: the NHS names wholemeal sliced bread, wholegrain or higher-fibre breakfast cereals and baked beans.
pages.alt: Smoked salmon, egg and cucumber on two slices of rye bread

source.name: Harvard Nutrition Source: Processed foods and health

pages.question: Tinned fish, some cheeses and freshly made bread sit in which NOVA group?
pages.explanation: Group 3 is processed: foods from groups 1 and 2 with salt, sugar or fat added.

source.name: Harvard Nutrition Source: Processed foods and health

steps.text: Read the first 3 ingredients: they're listed by weight, most first.
For bread, look for wholegrain flour as ingredient number 1.
Compare 2 cereals and choose the one with less added sugar, such as plain oats.
Cook 1 big batch and freeze the extra as ready meals.

source.name: Harvard Nutrition Source: Processed foods and health

pages.headline: Mostly unprocessed, room for the rest
pages.body: Harvard's general rule: build the day mostly on unprocessed or minimally processed foods; some processed products can be a useful addition. Two of its tips: cook at home from fresh ingredients, and cook in bulk to freeze.
pages.alt: Minestrone with beans, pasta and dark greens in a white bowl

source.name: Harvard Nutrition Source: Processed foods and health

pages.text: Building most meals from unprocessed or minimally processed foods leaves room for the rest.

lessons.title: Reading a label in 20 seconds
lessons.subtitle: Per 100 g, four numbers, the colours, the ingredients
lessons.coverBrief: Top-down overhead photo, camera pointing straight down, of four small plain matte white round ceramic bowls in a neat row: golden olive oil, a pale yellow pat of butter, white granulated sugar and coarse white sea salt, on a seamless pale cream background, soft diffused daylight, faint soft shadows under the bowls. Nothing else in frame. 3:2 landscape, photorealistic editorial food photography, sharp, natural colours.

source.name: BDA Food Fact Sheet: Food labelling

pages.headline: Start with the per 100 g column
pages.body: To compare two foods, use the per 100 g figures on the label. A serving may differ from what you eat: if it's 1 biscuit and you have 2, double the numbers.
pages.alt: Golden granola clusters spread out on a white plate

steps.text: Total fat: 3 g or less is low; more than 17.5 g is high.
Saturates: 1.5 g or less is low; more than 5 g is high.
Sugars: 5 g or less is low; more than 22.5 g is high.
Salt: 0.3 g or less is low; more than 1.5 g is high.

pages.headline: Red, amber, green
pages.body: Many packs show these cut-offs on the front as colours: red is high, amber neither high nor low, green low. Choosing between similar products? More greens and ambers is the healthier pick.

pages.question: A cereal has 25 g of sugars per 100 g. Which colour is that?
pages.explanation: More than 22.5 g of sugars per 100 g is high, so it shows red.

pages.headline: Ingredients run heaviest first
pages.body: Ingredients are listed by weight, the main ones first. If the first few are high-fat ones such as cream, butter or oil, the food is likely high in fat. Allergens are highlighted in bold.
pages.alt: Oats, raisins and sugar in three piles, largest to smallest

pages.question: On an ingredients list, which ingredient is there most of?
pages.explanation: Ingredients are listed by weight, most first; bold marks the allergens.

steps.text: 5 seconds: turn the pack over and find the per 100 g column.
5 seconds: read 4 numbers — total fat, saturates, sugars and salt.
5 seconds: on the front, count the reds, ambers and greens.
5 seconds: read the first 3 ingredients, the main ones by weight.

source.name: BDA Food Fact Sheet: Food labelling

pages.question: Two yoghurts come in different pot sizes. Which figures compare them fairly?
pages.explanation: Per 100 g puts both on the same footing, whatever the pot size.

pages.text: Compare per 100 g, check fat, saturates, sugars and salt, then read the first three ingredients.

lessons.title: Hydration and drinks
lessons.subtitle: Water, coffee, and what alcohol adds
lessons.coverBrief: Top-down overhead photo, camera pointing straight down, of one clear glass of still water with three ice cubes and one thin lemon slice, standing on one plain matte white round ceramic saucer, on a seamless pale cream background, soft diffused daylight, faint soft shadow. Nothing else in frame. 3:2 landscape, photorealistic editorial food photography, sharp, natural colours.

pages.headline: Tea and coffee count too
pages.body: The NHS suggests 6 to 8 cups or glasses of fluid a day. Water, lower-fat milk and lower-sugar drinks all count, tea and coffee included. Pee that's a clear pale yellow says you're drinking enough.
pages.alt: A cup of black coffee and a cup of tea with milk

steps.text: Spread 6–8 cups or glasses of fluid through the day.
Keep fruit juice and smoothies to 1 small glass, 150 ml, with a meal.
Drink more in 4 cases: heat, long activity, illness, pregnancy or breastfeeding.
Not keen on water? Try sparkling, or add 1 slice of lemon or lime.

pages.headline: Caffeine in a cup, roughly
pages.body: EFSA finds up to 400 mg a day, spread out, raises no safety concern for healthy adults; in pregnancy, 200 mg. For children and teenagers, its level is 3 mg per kg of body weight a day.

pages.question: For healthy adults, how much caffeine a day does EFSA find raises no safety concern?
pages.explanation: Up to 400 mg a day, spread out, for healthy adults; 200 mg in pregnancy.

pages.headline: What alcohol adds, in kcal
pages.body: Alcohol has 7 kcal a gram, almost as many as fat, and mixers such as cola or tonic add more. The beer and wine here are the NHS's highest figures.

pages.question: Gram for gram, alcohol has almost as many kcal as which?
pages.explanation: Alcohol has 7 kcal a gram, says the NHS, almost as many as fat.

pages.text: Water, lower-fat milk, tea and coffee all count towards 6–8 glasses of fluid a day.

lessons.title: Hunger, fullness and sleep
lessons.subtitle: What keeps you full, and how sleep plays in
lessons.coverBrief: Top-down overhead photo, camera pointing straight down, of one plain matte white round ceramic bowl of thick red lentil and chickpea stew with whole chickpeas, topped with a spoonful of plain white yoghurt and torn fresh coriander leaves, on a seamless pale cream background, soft diffused daylight, faint soft shadow under the bowl. Nothing else in frame. 3:2 landscape, photorealistic editorial food photography, sharp, natural colours.

pages.headline: Protein keeps you full for longer
pages.body: Chicken, beef, fish, beans and other high-protein foods leave the stomach more slowly. Slower emptying means you feel full for longer and get hungry later.
pages.alt: Chicken, rice, black beans, sweetcorn and avocado in a white bowl

source.name: Harvard Nutrition Source: Legumes and pulses

pages.headline: Fibre slows the meal down
pages.body: Fibre takes longer to chew, which slows your eating pace, and it slows digestion in the stomach: both may help you feel full. Beans, lentils and chickpeas bring protein and fibre together.
pages.alt: Beef chilli with kidney beans over rice, with soured cream

pages.question: Why do beans and chicken keep you full for longer?
options: They leave the stomach more slowly
pages.explanation: High-protein foods move more slowly from the stomach to the intestine, so hunger comes back later.

pages.headline: Short sleep, bigger appetite
pages.body: With too little sleep, the hunger hormone ghrelin tends to rise and leptin, which signals “stop eating”, to fall. Adults kept short of sleep in studies were hungrier and ate more, though not every study agrees.
pages.alt: A white mug of warm milk on a saucer

steps.text: Sensitive to caffeine? Leave 4–6 hours between your last coffee or tea and bed.
Finish a large meal or heavy snack 2–3 hours before bed.
Keep 7 or more hours a night for sleep: the adult recommendation.

pages.headline: Eat slowly, notice full
pages.body: Eat slowly and you're more likely to notice when you're satisfied. In a review of studies, slower eaters felt fuller sooner. Harvard's tips: small bites, chewed well, and no screen or work call at the table.
pages.alt: Quinoa salad with herbs and sliced chicken in a white bowl

pages.question: After short sleep, what do studies often find?
pages.explanation: Sleep-restricted adults were hungrier and ate more, though some studies found no change.

source.name: Harvard Nutrition Source: Legumes and pulses

pages.text: Protein and fibre help you feel full, and a slower meal helps you notice it.
